concepts.gdp_qoq: Real GDP growth (% q/q, not annualised)
concepts.fx_usd: Exchange rate against the US dollar ($ per £ / €)
concepts.cpi_yoy: Headline consumer price inflation (% y/y; HICP for euro area)
concepts.yield_2y_5y: Short-dated government bond yield (US 2y, UK 5y, EA 2y AAA, %)
concepts.debt_gdp: Government debt, % of GDP (US federal gross, UK public sector net, euro area general government gross)
concepts.border: Irregular arrivals (US southwest border encounters vs UK small boat arrivals, thousands per month)

about.what: The change in the prices of a basket of consumer goods and services over the past 12 months, measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
about.why: The best-known US inflation gauge. It moves Treasury yields, the dollar and expectations for Fed rate decisions, and it sets cost-of-living adjustments for Social Security.

about.what: CPI inflation excluding food and energy, whose prices swing with weather and oil markets.
about.why: Shows the underlying trend in inflation. A surprise in core usually matters more to markets than the headline figure.

about.what: Inflation in personal consumption expenditures excluding food and energy, measured by the Bureau of Economic Analysis. It covers a wider range of spending than CPI and adjusts as people switch between products.
about.why: The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure: its 2% target is defined on PCE, so this is the number the Fed watches most closely.

about.what: The change in the inflation-adjusted value of everything the US economy produces, compared with the previous quarter and expressed as an annual rate (roughly four times the quarterly change).
about.why: The broadest measure of whether the economy is growing. Two negative quarters is the popular definition of a recession, though in the US recessions are dated by the NBER.

indicators.name: Real GDP growth (not annualised)
indicators.note: Quarter-on-quarter change in real GDP, not annualised, so it is comparable with UK and euro area figures.

about.what: The quarter-on-quarter change in US real GDP without annualising, so it can be compared directly with UK and euro area growth.
about.why: Use this one to compare growth across countries; the headline US figure is annualised and looks about four times bigger.

about.what: The monthly change in the dollar value of sales at retailers and food services, adjusted for seasonal patterns but not for inflation.
about.why: Consumer spending is around two-thirds of the US economy, so this is an early read on how strongly households are spending.

about.what: The change over 12 months in the real output of US factories, mines and utilities, published by the Federal Reserve.
about.why: Industry is a small share of GDP but swings more than services, so it often turns first in a slowdown.

about.what: The University of Michigan's survey of how US households feel about their finances and the economy (1966 = 100). It also asks about expected inflation.
about.why: Sentiment can lead spending, and the survey's inflation expectations are watched closely by the Fed.

about.what: The share of the labour force (people working or looking for work) who are out of work and actively looking, from the monthly household survey.
about.why: One half of the Fed's mandate is maximum employment. A rising rate is one of the clearest signs of a weakening economy.

about.what: The monthly change in the number of people on non-farm payrolls, from the survey of employers. Released on the first Friday of most months.
about.why: Usually the most market-moving US data release: it's the most timely, broad read on hiring.

about.what: The change over 12 months in average hourly earnings of private-sector workers.
about.why: Fast wage growth can keep services inflation high; the Fed watches it to judge whether the labour market is overheating.

about.what: The number of people filing a first claim for unemployment insurance in the week, seasonally adjusted. Published every Thursday.
about.why: The most timely labour market data: a sustained rise in claims is an early warning of layoffs.

about.what: The upper end of the Federal Reserve's target range for the federal funds rate, the overnight rate at which banks lend to each other.
about.why: The Fed's main tool. It feeds through to mortgage, loan and savings rates and to every asset priced in dollars.

about.what: The yield on 2-year US Treasury notes.
about.why: Closely tracks where markets expect Fed policy to be over the next two years, so it moves sharply on data surprises.

about.what: The yield on 10-year US Treasury notes.
about.why: The benchmark for mortgages and long-term borrowing worldwide. It reflects expected rates, inflation and a premium for holding long-dated debt.

about.what: The change in the prices of a basket of consumer goods and services over the past 12 months, measured by the ONS.
about.why: The Bank of England's 2% target is defined on CPI. It moves gilt yields, sterling and expectations for Bank Rate.

about.what: CPI inflation excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco.
about.why: Shows underlying price pressure. The Bank of England also watches services inflation within it closely.

about.what: CPI plus owner-occupiers' housing costs (based on the rent equivalent) and council tax. The ONS's lead measure of inflation.
about.why: A fuller picture of household costs than CPI, though the Bank of England targets CPI.

about.what: The change in the inflation-adjusted value of everything the UK economy produces, compared with the previous quarter.
about.why: The broadest measure of UK growth. Two consecutive negative quarters is the usual definition of a technical recession.

about.what: The month-on-month change in UK GDP. The UK is one of few countries to publish a monthly estimate.
about.why: Gives an early read on the quarter, but it is volatile: strikes, weather and bank holidays can swing a single month.

about.what: The change over 12 months in the volume of goods sold by retailers in Great Britain, adjusted for prices.
about.why: An early, if volatile, read on consumer spending.

about.what: The share of the economically active population aged 16+ who are unemployed, from the Labour Force Survey, averaged over three months.
about.why: A key input to the Bank of England's view of spare capacity. The survey has had low response rates recently, so the ONS treats it with caution.

about.what: The share of people aged 16 to 64 who are in work, averaged over three months.
about.why: Complements the unemployment rate: it also captures people leaving the labour force altogether.

about.what: The change in average weekly earnings excluding bonuses, three months compared with a year earlier.
about.why: The Bank of England watches pay closely because it drives services inflation.

about.what: The interest rate the Bank of England pays on reserves held by commercial banks, set by the Monetary Policy Committee.
about.why: Drives mortgage, loan and savings rates across the UK.

about.what: The yield on 5-year UK government bonds (gilts), from the Bank of England's yield curve.
about.why: Tracks where markets expect Bank Rate to be, and feeds directly into the cost of fixed-rate mortgages.

about.what: The yield on 10-year gilts.
about.why: The government's long-term borrowing cost, watched closely around Budgets and fiscal announcements.

about.what: How many US dollars one pound buys (daily spot rate, Bank of England).
about.why: Reflects relative growth and interest rate expectations. A weaker pound raises import prices and inflation.

indicators.name: Public sector net borrowing
indicators.note: Excluding public sector banks. Positive = borrowing.

about.what: Public sector net borrowing excluding public sector banks, summed over the last 12 months: the gap between what the state spends and what it raises.
about.why: The rolling total smooths out monthly noise and shows whether the deficit is trending up or down against the Office for Budget Responsibility's forecasts.

indicators.name: Monthly borrowing
indicators.note: Not seasonally adjusted: compare with the same month a year earlier.

about.what: Public sector net borrowing in a single month. Not seasonally adjusted: January is usually a surplus because of self-assessment tax receipts.
about.why: Compared with the same month last year and with the OBR's forecast, it shows whether the public finances are on track ahead of fiscal events.

about.what: Public sector net debt excluding public sector banks, as a share of annual GDP.
about.why: One of the measures the government's fiscal rules have been set against.

about.what: The federal budget deficit over the last 12 months, from the Treasury's Monthly Treasury Statement.
about.why: Larger deficits mean more Treasury issuance, which can push up long-term yields.

indicators.name: Federal debt
indicators.note: Total public debt (gross, including intragovernmental holdings).

about.what: Total federal public debt, including debt held by government trust funds, as a share of GDP.
about.why: A broad gauge of the US fiscal position; the debt ceiling and rating agency actions focus on it.

indicators.name: Southwest border encounters
indicators.note: CBP: Border Patrol apprehensions + Office of Field Operations inadmissibles + Title 42 expulsions.

about.what: Encounters with migrants at the US southwest land border: Border Patrol apprehensions between ports of entry plus inadmissible people stopped at ports by the Office of Field Operations.
about.why: The most-watched measure of irregular migration to the US; it shifts quickly with policy changes.

indicators.name: Nationwide encounters
indicators.note: All CBP encounters: southwest, northern and coastal borders and ports of entry.

about.what: All CBP encounters across the southwest, northern and coastal borders and airports.
about.why: A wider view than the southwest border alone.

indicators.name: Foreign-born labour force
indicators.note: CPS household survey, not seasonally adjusted.

about.what: The change over 12 months in the number of foreign-born people in the US labour force, from the household survey.
about.why: Immigration has been a big driver of US labour supply, and so of how fast the economy can grow without overheating.

about.what: The unemployment rate among foreign-born workers (not seasonally adjusted).
about.why: Shows how well recent arrivals are being absorbed into work.

about.what: The change over 12 months in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices for the euro area, measured by Eurostat.
about.why: The ECB's 2% target is defined on HICP. The flash estimate at the start of each month moves bond yields and the euro.

indicators.name: Core HICP inflation
indicators.note: Excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco.

about.what: HICP inflation excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco.
about.why: The ECB's main read on underlying inflation.

about.what: Inflation in the services part of the HICP basket.
about.why: Services prices are driven by wages, so the ECB watches this to judge whether inflation is sticky.

about.what: The change in euro area real GDP compared with the previous quarter.
about.why: The broadest measure of euro area growth; the flash estimate comes out about 30 days after the quarter ends.

about.what: The change over 12 months in euro area industrial output (mining, manufacturing and energy).
about.why: Industry is a bigger share of the economy in Germany and Italy than in the US or UK, so it matters more here.

about.what: The change over 12 months in the volume of euro area retail trade.
about.why: A read on household spending across the bloc.

about.what: The European Commission's Economic Sentiment Indicator, combining business and consumer surveys (long-run average = 100).
about.why: Timely and closely linked to GDP growth: readings below 100 mean below-average confidence.

about.what: The share of the euro area labour force who are unemployed, measured by Eurostat.
about.why: The euro area jobs market has stayed tight even as growth slowed, which has kept wage growth and services inflation up.

about.what: The rate the ECB pays banks on overnight deposits. It's the rate the ECB uses to steer policy.
about.why: Sets short-term borrowing costs across the 21 countries that use the euro.

indicators.name: 2-year AAA govt yield
indicators.note: ECB euro area AAA-rated government yield curve (spot rate).

about.what: The 2-year yield on the ECB's curve built from AAA-rated euro area government bonds.
about.why: Tracks expected ECB policy, like the 2-year Treasury in the US.

indicators.name: 10-year AAA govt yield
indicators.note: ECB euro area AAA-rated government yield curve (spot rate).

about.what: The 10-year yield on the ECB's AAA-rated government curve, close to the German 10-year Bund.
about.why: The euro area's benchmark long-term rate; spreads of Italy, France and others are measured against it.

about.what: How many US dollars one euro buys (ECB reference rate).
about.why: The world's most traded currency pair, reflecting growth and rate differences between the euro area and the US.

about.what: Euro area general government gross debt (the Maastricht definition) as a share of GDP.
about.why: EU fiscal rules use a 60% of GDP reference value for debt.

about.what: The euro area general government deficit as a share of GDP, averaged over four quarters.
about.why: EU fiscal rules use a 3% of GDP reference value for deficits.

indicators.name: Small boat arrivals
indicators.note: Home Office: migrants detected crossing the English Channel. Provisional; complete months only.

about.what: The number of people detected crossing the English Channel in small boats each month, from Home Office daily figures.
about.why: The most politically watched measure of irregular migration to the UK. Crossings are very seasonal, so compare with the same month a year earlier.

about.what: Small boat arrivals summed over the last 12 months.
about.why: Removes the strong seasonal pattern to show the underlying trend.

indicators.name: Net migration
indicators.note: ONS provisional long-term international migration; rolling year ending in the month shown. Revised at every release.

about.what: Long-term immigration minus emigration over the 12 months to the date shown, provisional ONS estimates.
about.why: Drives UK population and labour supply. Figures are revised, often substantially, as more data comes in.

indicators.name: Asylum claims
indicators.note: People claiming asylum, including dependants (Home Office).

about.what: People claiming asylum in the UK each quarter, including dependants.
about.why: Determines demand on the asylum system and accommodation costs.

indicators.name: Work, study & family visas issued
indicators.note: Entry clearance visas issued (excludes visitor visas). Seasonal: study peaks in Q3.

about.what: Entry clearance visas issued each quarter for work, study and family reasons (visitor visas excluded).
about.why: A leading indicator of legal immigration, and so of future net migration.

US|PPI.what: Producer Price Index: the prices US producers receive for goods and services.
US|PPI.why: Some PPI components feed into the Fed's preferred PCE inflation measure, so it helps forecast PCE after CPI.

US|JOLTS job openings.what: Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey: job vacancies, hires, quits and layoffs.
US|JOLTS job openings.why: Openings relative to unemployed people show how tight the labour market is; the quits rate signals workers' confidence.

US|Housing starts.what: The number of new homes on which building started, and permits issued, in the month.
US|Housing starts.why: Housing is sensitive to mortgage rates, so it shows how monetary policy is feeding through.

US|Trade balance.what: Exports minus imports of goods and services.
US|Trade balance.why: Net trade feeds into GDP and can swing quarterly growth, especially around tariff changes.

US|Factory orders / durable goods.what: New orders, shipments and inventories at US manufacturers.
US|Factory orders / durable goods.why: Orders for capital goods are a proxy for business investment plans.

UK|PPI.what: Producer price inflation: the prices of materials bought and goods sold by UK manufacturers.
UK|PPI.why: Changes in input costs tend to feed through to consumer prices with a lag.

UK|Trade.what: UK exports and imports of goods and services.
UK|Trade.why: A component of GDP; also tracks trade with the EU and the effect of tariffs.

UK|Visa applications (monthly).what: Monthly applications for entry clearance visas, by route, from the Home Office.
UK|Visa applications (monthly).why: The most timely sign of where legal migration is heading, ahead of the quarterly statistics.

UK|Public sector finances.what: Monthly ONS and OBR figures on government receipts, spending, borrowing and debt.
UK|Public sector finances.why: Shows whether the government is on track to meet its fiscal rules, especially in the run-up to Budgets.
